content.p: On Sunday 19 October 2025, in daylight, four men reached an upper-floor balcony of the Louvre in Paris, the world's most-visited museum, using a furniture lift mounted on a truck. Two of them cut their way into the Apollo Gallery, and the team left within minutes with pieces of the French crown jewels. The haul was valued at an estimated 88 million euros, about $102 million, and that figure does not count the historical value of the objects. Within weeks, investigators had charged four men said to have made up the raiding team and a woman accused of complicity. The jewels have not been recovered, and none of those charged has been reported convicted.
content.h2: Seven minutes in the Apollo Gallery
content.p: NBC News described a "monte-meubles", a truck carrying a basket lift, that the thieves used to reach a balcony without, apparently, drawing the attention of police or security. According to NPR, the men wore reflective vests to look like maintenance workers. Laurence des Cars, the museum's director, told senators that they had put bollards out on the pavement as if they were carrying out works. Senators asked how a truck with a hoist could park against the museum wall, facing the wrong way and on a pavement, for two hours without anyone intervening.

Two of the men climbed up, broke a window and entered the gallery, setting off the alarms. NBC News reported that they threatened guards, and NPR said they cut into glass cases with a circular saw. A museum guard filmed part of the raid. The two men then climbed back down and left on motor scooters ridden by the other two members of the team. The whole operation took about seven minutes, according to CNN and the Guardian; Al Jazeera said less than eight and NPR less than ten. Franceinfo reported that the scooters followed the Seine quays to the ring road and then the A6 motorway.

Reports differ on how many pieces were taken: eight according to NBC News and Al Jazeera, and nine according to CNN and franceinfo. Among them were a diamond and sapphire set worn by Queen Marie-Amélie and Queen Hortense and an emerald and diamond necklace that Napoleon I gave his second wife, Marie Louise. The most valuable item the thieves dropped in their haste was the imperial crown of Empress Eugénie, set with 1,354 diamonds and 56 emeralds. It was found outside the museum. Des Cars told senators it had been damaged not by the fall but when the thieves tried to pull it through a gap in the case that was too small for it, and that a delicate restoration looked possible.

The escape left a trail. NPR listed what the thieves left behind in their hurry: a motorcycle helmet, a saw, a glove, fuel, a radio and a high-visibility vest. Franceinfo listed a walkie-talkie, gloves, a jerrycan, a blanket, a blowtorch and the disc cutter left on the lift. Des Cars said that private security guards outside who heard the alerts on their radios ran to the van and stopped the thieves from setting fire to it, which helped preserve evidence.

About 60 investigators were working on the case two days after the raid, franceinfo reported. On the evening of Saturday 25 October, according to prosecutor Laure Beccuau, two men were arrested within an hour of each other. One, a 34-year-old Algerian national who has lived in France since 2010, was stopped at Charles de Gaulle airport as he was about to leave for Algeria on a one-way ticket. He lives in Aubervilliers, north of Paris, and was known to police mainly for traffic offences and one theft. Beccuau said his DNA matched a scooter used in the getaway. The second man, 39, was arrested at his home, also in Aubervilliers. Beccuau said his DNA was found on one of the glass display cases and on items the thieves left behind, and that he had previous convictions for aggravated robbery in 2008 and 2014.

Beccuau said investigators had to move earlier than they wanted because one suspect appeared to be leaving the country. Investigators had earlier told ABC News that the second man was arrested as he was about to travel to Mali, but at her press conference on 29 October Beccuau said he had no intention of leaving the country. Both men gave "minimalist" statements and "partially admitted" their involvement, she said. On 29 October the prosecutor said they were to be brought before magistrates, and ABC News reported that both had been charged with organised theft, which carries up to 15 years in prison, and criminal conspiracy, which carries up to 10. Both were remanded in custody. French law keeps investigations secret, and only the prosecutor may speak publicly about them, so none of those arrested has been publicly named.

Five more people were arrested on Wednesday 29 October. Two of them were charged on Saturday 1 November. A 37-year-old man was charged with organised theft and criminal conspiracy, and ABC7 reported that he is believed to be the third member of the raiding team. ABC7 reported that his criminal record included 11 convictions, ten of them for theft, and that he and the 39-year-old were convicted in the same theft case in 2015. A 38-year-old woman, his longtime partner, with whom he has children, was charged with complicity. Her DNA was found in small quantity on the lift, which the prosecutor said might be explained by DNA transfer. NPR said the two were identified through DNA and cell phone records. Both denied any involvement, the prosecutor said. The woman's lawyer, Adrien Sorrentino, told reporters she was "devastated" and contested the charges. The other three people arrested that day were released without charge.

Beccuau told the radio network franceinfo that the raid was "not quite everyday delinquency" but a type that is not generally associated with the "upper echelons of organised crime". She described those charged as local people from Seine-Saint-Denis, a département north of Paris and one of the poorest in France. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said investigators were also looking for whoever might have ordered it.

On 25 November the prosecutor's office told CNN that four more people from the Paris region had been detained: men of 38 and 39 and women of 31 and 40. The last suspected member of the team was arrested at a construction site in Laval, in western France, according to a source close to the case cited by Al Jazeera. On Friday 28 November Beccuau announced that a 39-year-old man with six previous convictions, for offences including pimping, driving without a licence and receiving stolen goods, had been charged with organised theft and criminal conspiracy. The prosecutor said nothing about his role. Al Jazeera reported that the four suspected members of the raiding team had now all been arrested and charged, two of them having entered the gallery while two stayed outside. It added that the 38-year-old woman had been released on bail. Al Jazeera gave the ages of the men already held as 35, 37 and 39, whereas the prosecutor's statement earlier had put one of them at 34.

Finding the jewels has proved harder than finding the suspects. Beccuau told a press conference on 29 October that the jewels were "now, of course, unsellable" because anyone buying them would be guilty of concealing stolen goods, and she said there was "still time to give them back". She also told RTL that the thieves would not earn 88 million euros if they took the pieces apart, and she hoped they would not destroy them for no reason. Experts quoted by CNN feared the jewels might have been melted down and sold on, while others thought that was less likely given how quickly suspects were caught. On 2 November Beccuau said that investigators were examining the parallel market for selling such jewellery, which she said could be used for money laundering or trade.

The latest reports from late November 2025 still gave no sign of where the jewels are. A later franceinfo headline said that the Apollo Gallery had reopened without its jewels nine months after the burglary. No trial date has been reported.

The raid became a national argument about museum security almost at once. Des Cars, appearing before the Senate on 22 October, called it a "terrible failure". She said every alarm had worked, but that the only camera covering that side of the building faced west and did not cover the balcony the thieves used, and she called camera cover of the outer walls "highly insufficient". She had tendered her resignation after the burglary, she said, and Culture Minister Rachida Dati refused it. She defended the museum's 80 million euro security plan against a report citing persistent delays.

Paris Police Chief Patrice Faure told the Senate that the museum's video network was still partly analogue and that a promised overhaul would not be finished before 2029 or 2030. He disclosed that the Louvre's authorisation to operate its security cameras had lapsed in July without being renewed. Faure said police arrived extremely fast, but that the delay came earlier in the chain, from first detection through the museum's security and the emergency line to police command. The call that first alerted police, he and his team said, was made not because of the museum's alarms but by a cyclist outside who saw helmeted men with a basket lift.

NPR reported that des Cars also admitted that only a third of the museum's wings were under video surveillance. Just before those charges, Dati presented the first findings of an inspection by cultural affairs inspectors. It spoke of a "chronic, structural underestimation of the risk of intrusion and theft at the Louvre for the last 20 years". President Emmanuel Macron called the raid "an attack on a heritage that we cherish because it is our history" and vowed that the perpetrators would be brought to justice. Beccuau, for her part, complained about leaks to the French press, saying that hasty disclosure by people who knew about the case could hinder the investigation.
